source.text: וַ/יֹּאמַ֗ר יְהוָ֞ה מִ/סִּינַ֥י בָּא֙ וְ/זָרַ֤ח מִ/שֵּׂעִיר֙ לָ֔/מוֹ הוֹפִ֨יעַ֙ מֵ/הַ֣ר פָּארָ֔ן וְ/אָתָ֖ה מֵ/רִבְבֹ֣ת קֹ֑דֶשׁ מִֽ/ימִינ֕/וֹ אשדת לָֽ/מוֹ׃

translation.text: And he said: “Yahweh came from Sinai and dawned from Seir upon them; he shone forth from Mount Paran, and came from holy myriads[a]; from his right hand came a fiery law[b] for them.”

footnotes.text: Hebrew literally 'myriads of holiness'; also understood as 'myriads of holy ones.' 'Holy myriads' preserves their holy character without settling whether heavenly or human attendants are meant.

Hebrew אשדת is obscure. 'Fiery law' follows the Masoretic reading as 'fire' and 'law'; an alternative verbal analysis yields 'fire flew,' while the selected Greek text has 'angels with him.' The original meaning remains unresolved.

lexical_decisions.rationale: Per doctrine, the Tetragrammaton יְהוָה is rendered 'Yahweh' — the transliteration of the divine name — rather than the traditional 'the LORD' substitution. This preserves the personal name God revealed to Israel rather than substituting a title.
בּוֹא in the qatal here describes YHWH's advent/appearance. 'Came from Sinai' is natural English and preserves the directional force of מִן.

lexical_decisions.chosen: and dawned from Seir upon them
alternatives: and rose from Seir for them
and shone from Seir upon them
lexical_decisions.rationale: זָרַח commonly refers to the rising/shining of light, especially like the sun. 'Dawned' preserves the poetic imagery better than a flatter 'rose.' לָמוֹ is rendered 'upon them' here to fit the theophanic imagery of light breaking over the people.
The hiphil of יפע carries the sense of shining forth or appearing radiantly. 'Shone forth' keeps both the visual and the poetic force.

alternatives: from the hill country of Paran
lexical_decisions.rationale: הַר is straightforwardly 'mountain/mount.' 'Mount Paran' is the conventional and clear rendering for the place name construction.
The verb denotes coming/approaching. 'Came' maintains the parallel sequence of divine advent verbs in the verse.

alternatives: from ten thousands of holy ones
lexical_decisions.rationale: The singular holiness noun qualifies myriads. A quality-genitive rendering preserves their holy character without forcing angelic or human identity; the close abstract gloss and holy-ones interpretation are noted. This is a provisional rendering of unchanged pointed WLC, not a change to plural qadoshim. Meaning takes priority over an English calque that suggests counted units of holiness.
The preposition מִן most naturally means 'from.' 'From his right hand' fits the imagery of what proceeds from YHWH in the next phrase.

alternatives: fire flew for them (alternative verbal analysis)
lexical_decisions.rationale: Provisional qere-based interpretation: actual WLC reads fire and law as two words, while the saved source retains written ashdat. The Sinai context and explicit Torah in verse4 permit a law association, but do not prove original meaning. Actual BDB fire/law sections discuss lexical difficulty and conjectural emendations. Alternative fire-flew morphology and the Greek angel clause require separate source interpretation; neither is a simple synonym for this fixed qere. No original-priority victory or fresh HALOT consultation is claimed.
The pronominal form indicates third person plural. 'For them' reads naturally in English and suits the sense of something given on Israel's behalf.

theological_decisions.issue: Identity of the divine subject in a poetic theophany
theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Retain the already chosen divine name Yahweh and the poetic Sinai theophany without adding a later christological identification.
alternative_readings: Some Christian readings see typological anticipation of later divine revelation.
theological_decisions.rationale: The verse is a Mosaic blessing describing YHWH's theophanic coming from Sinai/Seir/Paran. The translation should preserve the OT context and not embed later theological interpretation into the wording itself.

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Render the unchanged phrase 'holy myriads,' disclosing the abstract close gloss and holy-ones interpretation without deciding heavenly versus human attendants.
theological_decisions.rationale: A qualitative rendering can be intelligible and preserve genuine uncertainty. Neither singular qodesh morphology nor contextual holy ones establishes an exclusive angelic identity. Greek Kades in the preceding colon is not direct lexical confirmation of this English choice.

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Retain 'a fiery law' provisionally as a Masoretic-qere interpretation, not a demonstrated earliest meaning.
alternative_readings: fire flew for them (alternative source analysis)
theological_decisions.rationale: Attested Greek and Latin interpretations differ. The inspected DSS tail is supplied and cannot decide them. Dat vocabulary and the proposed contraction remain disputed; the reader note exposes the conditional qere choice and serious alternatives. Familiarity alone is not the reason for retention.

revisions.from: And he said: “The LORD came from Sinai and dawned from Seir upon them; he shone forth from Mount Paran, and came from myriads of holiness; from his right hand came a fiery law for them.”
revisions.to: And he said: “The LORD came from Sinai and dawned from Seir upon them; he shone forth from Mount Paran, and came from myriads of holy ones; from his right hand came fiery bolts for them.”
revisions.rationale: Revised two phrases for lexical accuracy: changed 'myriads of holiness' to 'myriads of holy ones' and 'a fiery law' to 'fiery bolts,' which better reflects the difficult Hebrew here without importing an interpretive reading into the main text.

revisions.from: And he said: “Yahweh came from Sinai and dawned from Seir upon them[a]; he shone forth from Mount Paran, and came from myriads of holy ones[b]; from his right hand came fiery bolts for them.”
revisions.to: And he said: “Yahweh came from Sinai and dawned from Seir upon them[a]; he shone forth from Mount Paran, and came from myriads of holiness[b]; from his right hand came a fiery law for them.”
revisions.rationale: Azure substituted 'myriads of holy ones' (drafter's first rejected_alternative — drafter chose 'myriads of holiness' to preserve Hebrew ambiguity per DOCTRINE.md §3) and 'fiery bolts' (not even a documented alternative for אשדת — drafter chose tradition-conscious 'a fiery law' with uncertainty footnoted).

revisions.from: And he said: “Yahweh came from Sinai and dawned from Seir upon them[a]; he shone forth from Mount Paran, and came from myriads of holiness[b]; from his right hand came a fiery law for them.”
revisions.to: And he said: “Yahweh came from Sinai and dawned from Seir upon them; he shone forth from Mount Paran, and came from holy myriads[a]; from his right hand came a fiery law[b] for them.”
revisions.rationale: Provisional quality-genitive rendering on unchanged WLC; separately repair both note anchors and disclose qere/Greek/fire uncertainty. Retain historical drafts/reviews without transferring certification.

value.text: And he said: “Yahweh came from Sinai and dawned from Seir upon them[a]; he shone forth from Mount Paran, and came from myriads of holiness[b]; from his right hand came a fiery law for them.”

footnotes.text: Or 'from myriads of holy ones.' The Hebrew phrase may refer to holy attendants rather than abstract holiness.
Hebrew אשדת is difficult and uncertain; traditionally rendered 'a fiery law,' but it may also denote fiery flashes or fire proceeding from his right hand.

value.rationale: The Hebrew construction is difficult. קֹדֶשׁ can denote holiness or, by implication, holy beings/holy ones. Because the phrase is ambiguous and the following clause is also textually difficult, the main text keeps a more formally transparent rendering, while a footnote preserves the common interpretive alternative 'myriads of holy ones.'

This is a notoriously difficult form. The traditional Jewish/English rendering understands it as related to 'fire' plus 'law/decree' and fits the Sinai context. Because the form is uncertain, the choice is retained in the main text for readability and tradition-consciousness, with lexical uncertainty documented and alternatives footnoted.
The pronominal form indicates third person plural. 'For them' reads naturally in English and suits the sense of something given on Israel's behalf.

value.chosen_reading: Render the subject as the covenant God, 'the LORD,' without importing later christological interpretation into the translation.
alternative_readings: Some Christian readings see typological anticipation of later divine revelation.
value.rationale: The verse is a Mosaic blessing describing YHWH's theophanic coming from Sinai/Seir/Paran. The translation should preserve the OT context and not embed later theological interpretation into the wording itself.

value.chosen_reading: Keep an ambiguous main-text rendering ('myriads of holiness') and preserve 'myriads of holy ones' in a footnote.
value.rationale: The Hebrew permits more than one construal, and the phrase has interpretive significance for whether the scene includes angelic attendants. Per the translation philosophy, genuine ambiguity should be preserved rather than over-resolved.

value.chosen_reading: Use 'a fiery law' in the main text, with a footnote noting lexical uncertainty.
alternative_readings: flashing fire from his right hand
value.rationale: The form is obscure and has generated multiple explanations. 'A fiery law' is the longstanding and contextually coherent rendering in a Sinai setting, but the uncertainty should remain auditable and visible.
